newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Nowhere left for Afghans to run.
newsitem.headline: Nowhere left for Afghans to run.

text.p: Afghanistan has become a land of the lost, a doomed and near-forgotten people with nowhere left to run but the corners of their own war-scarred nation.

Now, as a decisive new battle looms for control of Kabul, capital of the land of writer Rudyard Kipling's "great game", many Afghans believe that whatever the result, they will simply have reached yet another crossroads to nowhere.

In just three decades, the land of many tribes and ethnic groups has gone through violent swings from monarchy to communism to present-day Islamic fundamentalism, a tortured journey that would leave any nation exhausted.
"We are a lost people," says Ibrahim, restaurant manager at this northern Afghan city's Hotel Mazar.

Ibrahim, for 20 years a barman at Kabul's Intercontinental Hotel, fled to Mazar-i-Sharif five years ago, joining thousands of people who left the capital when fighting broke out among rival factions in the Mujahideen alliance that took over the country when the former Soviet-backed government collapsed.
"I have nowhere to go after this," he says.
U.N. assessments of Afghanistan's future tell the same story.
The United Nations' latest so-called Human Development Index -- a ranking some diplomats call the "misery table" -- places Afghanistan 170th of 174 countries.
"It is the least developed country in the world outside Africa," a U.N. report said earlier this year.
U.N. statistics amply back up the grim assessment of a nation going nowhere.

The illiteracy rate is 75 percent, Afghanistan has one of the world's highest infant and maternal mortality rates, unemployment is over 50 percent, malnutrition grips 57 percent of the population, inflation is soaring past 500 percent and land under cultivation goes down every month.
The U.N. report said that in the 18 years since Soviet forces occupied Afghanistan, setting off the present spiral downwards, agricultural production has halved.
The overwhelming main crop grown on the halved land that remains is opium poppy -- shockingly, the underpinning of what is left of Afghanistan's ever declining economy.

The U.N. report said Afghanistan's opium prodution was equal to the combined production of the three other biggest opium producers in the world "with important consequences for the global consumption of heroin".
Strewn over Afghanistan's landscape are more than 10 million landmines, possibly the biggest concentration in the world, and daily taking a toll on the unwary..
The misery has added up to a massive refugee flight among Afghanistan's 17 million population.
International agencies estimate one million people in Afghanistan have fled their homes to other parts of the country. Another 1.4 million have sought refuge in Iran and 900,000 in Pakistan.

With flight from danger an ever present possibility, Afghanistan has become a land of single names where people prefer just to give one of their names to foreign journalists for fear of reprisal if the political wind shifts.

A de facto partition of the country is already under way. The so-called Northern Alliance of Tajiks, Uzbeks and Hazaras control areas of the country north of Kabul bordering Central Asian republics, issuing their own visa for foreigners.

At the gates of Kabul, where the next big battle is building, the Alliance faces Afghanistan's nominal government of the Taleban, an Islamic fundamentalist group that controls the capital and Pashtun areas bordering Pakistan.

"Zia", a former Afghan foreign ministry official in Kabul and now "chief protocol officer" for the Northern Alliance, says his group has the upper hand in the impending battle for Kabul which alliance commanders say could come as early as this week.
Zia laments that the international community has turned its back on his country's desperate plight.
"Bosnia has been solved, people are even talking in the Middle East," he says. "But our agony goes on."
Zia says that when the big powers -- the United States and the Soviet Union -- were involved in Afghanistan, the country's people were courted.
"Now, where are my friends abroad?" he asks. One is a taxi driver in New York, one works in an abattoir in Germany. Another works 16 hours a day in a factory in India.
"We have run out of places to run," he says. "Our fate is now just in our hands."

The possible coming battle for Kabul pits the purist Islamic Taleban against the Northern Alliance. The latter's main leaders are Tajik frontline commander Ahmed Shah Masood, a folklore hero of the battle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan, and General Abdul Malik, an enigmatic 37-year-old hereditary Uzbek warlord based in Mazar-i-Sharif, from where the alliance has launched bombing raids on Kabul in recent days.
The alliance wants a demilitarisation of Kabul as a condition for peace talks now being mediated by U.N. officials and neighbours of Afghanistan, including Pakistan and Iran.

But the Taleban, which controls more than two-thirds of the country, rejects the idea and wants the return of hundreds, or thousands, of its fighters, made prisoner when Malik drove it out of Mazar-i-Sharif after a short-lived alliance.

U.N. sources in Mazar-i-Sharif say that in verbal contacts, the Northern Alliance officials have suggested that its forces and Taleban forces should withdraw out of rocket range of the capital -- about 40 km (25 miles) -- as part of a demilitarisation plan for both sides, leaving the capital's security to a U.N. multinational force.

But the sources say that because of the U.N. budget problems and donor fatigue on Afghanistan, it would take far too long, up to six months, to put together a multinational force, even if there was the international will to do so.
The alternative, to put together an Afghan force acceptable to both sides, is regarded as completely impossible because of the distrust between the Afghan ethnic groups and warlords.
